utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all. I hope the interpreters can hear me well. Your Honours, I would like to raise an issue. As you've probably noticed my client is not here in the Courtroom with us today. So perhaps it might be a good idea to raise the issue in private session, since this concerns my client's health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would think you only need to mention the essential facts, Mr. Vasic. No need to go into details. So I think we can remain in public session. It's important that the public are aware if an accused is not in Court, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. But regrettably I'm not familiar with the detail of the matter. I just received word of this, this afternoon past one o'clock. All I know is that for the time being, Mr. Mrksic's situation does not appear to be critical, but that is all I know about his present condition or the doctor's predictions for that matter. This is not something that I have been informed of. Given the circumstances, I have not had an opportunity to see or meet Mr. Mrksic. All I've been told is that his health is not critical. It's fine compared to what it was. That's about all the detail I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. What has been heard by the Chamber takes the matter a little further. The information we have is that your client was undergoing some planned routine testing and it was found that that testing should be extended further. As he was then at the hospital, it was decided he should remain at the hospital to complete this further testing. And the expectation was that he would be with us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour, for sharing this with me. This is more than I know. I heard from Mr. Mrksic yesterday in the morning hours and he told me that he would be undergoing medical checks, that were scheduled. Or rather I didn't know about this at all and I was somewhat taken aback when I heard from the hospital today telling me that he had been hospitalized.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Well, as you have mentioned, a waiver has been filed, so the proceeding will continue today on that basis. Now you have a witness ready to call, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am ready to call my witness. That much is true. The waiver that you have addressed is not something that I've so far been able to look at. I suppose Mr. Mrksic has been informed of the relevant legal implications of his decision to have the trial continue in his absence. I do suppose that he has had an opportunity to express his own free will by signing the document that Your Honour has referred to. I wasn't there when the document was signed, nor have I seen the document. All I can say is that I'll try to take this in good faith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, we know nothing of the circumstances. We know that the document is filed. That is all we know. There has been experience in this trial of waiver by an accused in the trial proceeding in the absence of an accused, so that there is a basis upon which the Chamber can assume, at the moment, that your client is adequately aware of his rights and the effect of a waiver. In those circumstances, it would appear preferable that we should continue. Should it emerge that there is some unforeseen problem about the waiver, we will have to consider that. But that does not seem a likely possibility. So if you would call your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. Our next witness is Mr. Rade Danilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read out the affirmation that is on the card that is given to you now. RADE DANILOVIC: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can I have the Usher's assistance, please. I would like to distribute sets of documents to all the parties; documents we'll be using today. Part of the set is a hard copy of the war and operations log of the 80th Brigade and the LAD PVO order. You can put that aside for the time being, sir. We'll be using that later on. Thank you very much. I hope all copies have been distributed. Good afternoon, sir. Can you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Rade Danilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about your educational background, and where did you start with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in addition to secondary school, I completed a military academy and the command staff tactical school. I served in Selj [phoen] and Maribor, for as long as about 19 years, after which I got a transfer to Kragujevac where I stayed throughout. I spent some time at the front in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, I do have to ask you something.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You speak the same language as I do. And please make a pause after each of my questions before you embark on your answer in order to allow the interpreters sufficient time to interpret first the question and then your answer. Only what remains in the transcript is the record of this trial. I think the best thing to do, the best course of action to take would be for you to follow the cursor on the monitor in front of you. When you see a sentence end, when you see my question end, please start your answer. That perhaps might be the best idea. Another thing I would like to ask you is, when you speak, please speak at the same pace that I'm speaking now, so that the interpreters are allowed sufficient time to interpret your answers in their entirety, otherwise we'll be losing portions of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say you served in Slovenia as an officer. Up until which year specifically and where exactly was that? What were your positions as an officer? Your posts?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: [Realtime transcript read in error "Q."] In addition to being company commander, a position which I held for about eight years, the last positions I had in the division was as second in command operations officer, that was in 1990, before all the well known developments. On or about the 7th of October, there was an order from Belgrade from the personnel department, ordering my transfer to Kragujevac. I had to travel through Austria Hungary. I'd been ordered to report to the Sabac garrison after which I was told that I would be going to Kragujevac. I was supposed to take up the post of Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade once I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Again, can you just please hold a second after each of my questions, and one correction for the transcript. The witness's last answer, the record says question whereas in reality it was an answer, and that was because you were off the mark too fast, sir. Sir, you say you had to travel through Austria. Why did you take that route on your way to Kragujevac and who was the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, the unit that you just referred to at the time you arrived in Kragujevac and reported to start your service as Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I was compelled to travel through Austria and Hungary, given that all the communications to Belgrade, at least for us officers at that point in time -- other rather it wasn't possible for me to reach Sabac and that is why I decided to travel through Austria and Hungary; that seemed the safest route to take. Once I arrived, and I think this was on the 10th of October, 1991, I arrived in Kragujevac, Colonel Rakic told me that I had been appointed to serve as the Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade. He said the brigade had already been mobilised, and that I was to report to the Captain, to the commander lieutenant-colonel Vojnovic at Domatino [phoen] Polje, near Divcibare; this is a military training ground. On the 10th of October, I reported to the commander, to start work there as Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade, the position that I'd been appointed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. As for Commander Vojnovic, did you know him before your arrival in Kragujevac?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I knew Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic from my time in Slovenia. He at one time perhaps served in Slovenska Bistrica, in the garrison in Slovenska Bistrica while I was in Selj, and later, between 1987 and 1991, I served in the Maribor garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your capacity as Chief of Staff of the 80th Brigade, you continued to be a member of the command, right? Did you perhaps learn about Mr. Vojnovic's duties while he was in Slovenia and did he have any sort of military specialty, a special field of activity while he was there?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was an MP company commander. I also think that later he became the commander of a Partisan Brigade, but I'm not positive. And I'm not 100 per cent certain, just to be quite honest. We knew each other from large-scale officers' meetings, from briefings, from conferences in the JNA hall in Maribor, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say you arrived from the Motorised Brigade in 1980 and were part of its command back in 1991. Can you tell us whether this brigade, like its command, was trained to secure persons and facilities? Was it properly trained to carry out assignments like that, assignments of that nature?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: A lot of effort had been made to properly train both privates and officers for both combat operations and any other assignments typically carried out by Motorised Brigades in other similar units, which included providing security for persons and buildings, facilities. It was a well-known fact that the brigade was properly and sufficiently trained to carry out assignments of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us about the brigade's composition back in 1991 when the assignment arrived to go to the Vukovar front. Did it have any MP units, military police units, if so, what kind?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The 80th Brigade had a military police company, comprised of military police company. Normally all brigades have more or less the same sort of composition and all brigades normally comprise a military police company.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At one point in time did your brigade receive anything from the 24th Corps, an additional unit comprising MP officers?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: During the fighting in Vukovar the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade was reinforced with the military police company from the corps battalion of the military police, belonging to the 24th Kragujevac Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When the brigade received the assignment to go to the Vukovar front, what was the ethnic make up of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Based on my recollection, and it has been a long time, it has been 15 years, I think I can say that the brigade was multi-ethnic. The commander of the 105-millimetre HAD was Franjo Ekart, who I believe was an ethnic Croat. Then there was Jan Mancek, a Slovak. The chief of the medical corps, his name escapes me right now, but I know that he, too, was an ethnic Croat. And there were other ethnicities involved. So the brigade was a multi-ethnic one. That's one thing I can say with a great degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about this multi-ethnic makeup of the brigade, did that change before you set out for Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: How should I put this? The make up may have changed, but the changes were negligible, depending on the numbers of recruits responding to the last military call up, the last mobilisation call up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about all of these officers you mentioned a while ago as being non-Serbs, did they join the brigade on its way to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I think they were all off with the brigade to Vukovar with the exception of one officer from the medical corps, I think his name was Vinko, but I can't quite remember the reason behind him not going. I can't remember the reason he didn't join us on the way to Vukovar. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you remember pursuant to whose order and when the 80th Motorised Brigade was finally off to the Vukovar front?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see this specific order, but the brigade commander must have. The order was received from the command of the 24th Kragujevac corps which I suppose had, in turn, received the order to ensure the brigade's involvement through the command of the 1st Military District. I think that was the procedure that ought to have been applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard about several rounds of mobilisation from previous witnesses, as far as this unit was concerned. I'm going to talk about the third round, which is when the unit finally left for Vukovar. Early November 1991, did the entire unit go or just parts of the unit, just certain elements?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Due to the well-known problems involving certain parties that affected in a very powerful way the mood and the morale of the men belonging to the brigade, the brigade could not be introduced to the Vukovar front as a whole. For this reason, the third round, the third mobilisation round was away to introduce the brigade in successive stages, that is why the battalions and divisions were mobilised in order to bring them into the theatre at war. It was either on the 30th or on the 31st of October, 1991 that I went there with the 1st Motorised Battalion which at the time was led by Captain Susa. He was the battalion commander at the time. Later on, other elements and other units belonging to the brigade were mobilised and, roughly speaking, by the 10th of November I think they had all been brought in, or rather brought to the area where the 80th Motorised Brigade was performing operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We'll be looking at a number of documents addressing this issue, but first of all, let me ask you this. You mentioned the 1st Motorised Battalion, you mentioned your own departure on the 30th or 31st of October, 1991. Which area, exactly, did the battalion go to? And whose area of responsibility was that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Motorised Battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade was resubordinated to the Novi Sad Corps, we arrived in the Klis village area or Klis village sector, and I can't quite remember the specific units that it joined in the attack on Luzac village, but one thing I do know is the battalion was with me, because I was there with the commander of the first battalion. That was from the north. That was to the north of Vukovar and that's where their involvement began. That's where Luzac village was. Later on, the battalion continued attacks from the north on Vukovar, Vukovar's downtown area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the remaining elements of the 80th Motorised Brigade arrived in the broader Vukovar area you say by the 10th of November, 1991. Did this remaining part of the Motorised Brigade go all together? Or did they split up with separate elements arriving?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: These remaining elements belonging to the brigade were brought in, in portions, so to speak. There could have been two division, a battalion-level unit, for example, or one of the staff units. But they were brought in, in stages, as it were, to the area where the brigade was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have Exhibit 1D27 brought up on our screens, the ERN is 0D 000284. In the hand-outs that I distributed it is under 7, toward the end. At the end of that handout with the green tabs. Mr. Danilovic, what does this order mean? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: This is the order of the command of the 1st Army District, which was received by the command of the 24th Kragujevac Corps, that a platoon of ABC protection pioneer battalion and a support battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade from the garrison of Smederevo [phoen], should start their march in the direction of Smederevo, Beograd, and Niksic, Negoslavci and join the rest of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me when, on the basis of this order, the march was supposed to start, the march of these elements of the 80th Motorised Brigade that you mentioned and when were they supposed to arrive in the sector of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: According to this order, this march should have begun at 800 hours on November 10th, 1991, and the starting point is Smederevo barracks. I was then around the village of Luzac with the 1st Motorised Battalion, that is north of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know where you were. You had told us so. But I asked you when the march was supposed to begin according to this order and when the units, including the support units of the battalion were supposed to arrive at Vukovar, at the area of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot see any mention of these support units. Oh, yes, I'm sorry. By November 10th the support battalion should also have been there, deployed around the village of Sotin, I think, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I think that is clear enough. It's said in the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's, it slipped my mind. I failed to notice. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I propose to tender this order into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which tab did you say it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last tab, tab 27 in this series.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I heard -- apparently misheard. I thought you had said "7," and I had got lost. We will receive tab 27.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's exhibit 775, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me now ask you, Mr. Danilovic, whether the 80th Motorised Brigade included LAD PVO Artillery Battalion while the brigade was deployed at the Vukovar front.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The LAD PVO of the 80th Motorised Brigade was part of the brigade all the time. Occasionally, possibly a platoon or a battery of that artillery battalion may have been assigned to other units to reinforce Operational Group South. But as much time has passed, I cannot recollect for sure. I do know, however, that LAD PVO was not resubordinated to other units in the area covered by OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, from who did the commander of the LAD PVO battalion, while it was parts of the 80th Motorised Brigade around Vukovar received his orders?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of LAD PVO, exclusively received his orders from the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, which is clear due to the formational structure. However, if a part of this battalion was assigned to support other units, then the commander would receive relevant orders from his commander to redeploy parts of his -- parts of that artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As the head of staff, you -- and I'm now speaking in principle -- which were your tasks in the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The head of staff is a deputy -- is a deputy commander while the commander is absent. This is clear from the information. And now I don't think it is unnecessary to list all the persons that were members of the staff of the brigade, but the Chief of Staff or head of staff advises the commander on the deployment of the brigade. And he is the commander of the staff units of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As Chief of Staff you were well acquainted with the situation inside the unit while you were with the command of the 80th brigade, about the elements were part of the brigade, which elements were resubordinated. You were in a position to know that as Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had to know that, and I did know that. But from October 30th or 31st, 1991 until my arrival at the command of the brigade, I did not have knowledge of that kind because I had not yet joined the brigade proper. So for some 15 days or so, I was absent from there so that I'm not acquainted with the events during at that time. But when I arrived at the command of the brigade, I was partly acquainted with the events from the previous period, for the most important ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I propose that we now look at Exhibit 371, which is an operational log of the 80th Motorised Brigade. We have already looked at that log. Since the witness has a hard copy of the document in front of him, we could probably look at the English version of that document on our screens. It's D 000635. The entry refers to November 10th, 11.50, 11 hours 50 minutes. I will now read it out, Mr. Danilovic, and then ask you for your comment. It says: "The commander of LAD PVO and the head of PVO report. One, conscript wounded. From the second battery, 20/3 millimeters. The name is Jadranko, son of Milko, from Arandjelovac, and was admitted to the hospital of OG South. Tell me, as Chief of Staff, whether, in accordance with the rules of war, a unit that was resubordinated to another unit was supposed to report to its original brigade about such an event.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: If a unit that was part of our brigade was resubordinated to another unit, it must report to that other unit about its combat readiness and possible problems that may have arisen. It is possible and desirable also to report to its original unit or command, but it is not mandatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us continue with this log. November 13th, 1300 hours. We can look at the English version again. Page 0D 000636. Sir, please take a look at this entry. It says: LAD PVO, commander, report. It is necessary to -- we didn't understand the speaker. We missed communications equipment and shelter equipment. Is this a request for logistical support?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: From the -- that log entry it follows that the commander of LAD PVO requests the -- this equipment to be provided, and that is logical as the unit is an element of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. You said it was logical because a unit is an element of the brigade. I will now suggest to take a brief look at the next page, the entry for 1700 hours on November 14th, on the next page. The English translation of that page is 0D 000637. This says: "So far, regular combat reports have arrived from the following units: Headquarters, administration, the military police company, the ABC Protection Platoon, the Communications Company, LAD PVO, HAD 105, NPOAD and the 3rd Motorised Battalion." Tell me, please whose duty is it to submit regular reports to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Regular combat reports are submitted by all battalion commanders and the commanders of independent units likewise report to the head of staff on the situation in their units at the end of the day. That can be at 1700 hours or at 1800 hours. This depends on the command of the -- the order of the brigade commander so that he may, then, forward that to the his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that refer to the commanders of the units that are part of the 80th Brigade or other units, too?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: This applies to all units that are a part of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see the entry dated November 15th, 1991. 1700 hours. The English translation is on page 0 D 000637 -- sorry. 638. This says: "On review viewing the regular reports that were sent in by the 3rd Motorised Brigade, NPOAD, HAD, 105, LAD PVO, the Motor Police Company, and the ABC Defence Platoon, it can be concluded that there were no casualties in these units. Some of them were active ..." and so on. Is this entry also a regular combat report from the units that are part of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is clear that these regular reports were received from subordinate units to the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would now like to refer to another entry of that same day, November 15th, 1991, but at 2000 -- 20 hours and ten minutes, page 639 in the English translation. Mr. Danilovic, could you please comment the entry in the operational log. 20 hours, 10 minutes. "From the Mala Dubrava, Ovcara and Bokovci sectors, massive fire was open from infantry weapons, as well as from anti-aircraft guns. I warned the commanding officer not to open fire unless necessary. Everything calmed down by 2230 hours." Which unit was active there and who commanded to cease fire? Can you tell us, based on this entry?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Fire was opened. The units that were deployed in Mala Dubrava, Ovcara, and Bokovci, those were the units that opened fire, and it is logical --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were used on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: But this says that infantry weapons were used as well as anti-aircraft guns, this is what the operational log says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which units that were part of the 80th Motorised Brigade had anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, firstly, the LAD PVO had such guns. I cannot remember now, probably the armoured battalion also had some and possibly some other units, but I would need some time to think about it, to recollect. The infantry battalions such as the LAR platoon of PVO, I can't remember precisely, but I -- but several units had anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at the entry dated November 16th at 700 hours, 0D 000639 is the English page, the page of the English translation. It says: "After last night's intensive fire, the second half of the night was relatively calm. We had communications with all units in the wire communication system. Except for the LAD PVO. That link was down during the night." And the next entry for 9 hours 20 minutes on the same page is also linked to that. "I was informed that communications with the LAD PVO were established after a team went out to the field." Tell me, Mr. Danilovic, do these entries mean that the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade had communication at all times with the LAD PVO, except during the time when the link was down?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had come -- they could communication with each other. There were occasional problems with the communications, though. How do I put this? If there is a wire link and the wire is broken, possibly when a vehicle runs over it or for other reasons, such occasions did occur, but were remedied as soon as possible. It is obvious that we could communicate with LAD PVO, except for occasional blackouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Danilovic. Did you, at any moment, come to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade from the motorised battalion, and how long did you stay there, if you did?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, on November the 15th or the 16th I arrived at the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade at Negoslavci, and from that day until January 22nd, 1992, I was at the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade without interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After arriving at the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, were you in the position to access the data about the number of soldiers in that brigade and, what was the strength of that brigade when it was fully manned?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The strength of the 80th Motorised Brigade and its wartime formation is, I think, 4950, or 4920 men; thereabouts. After the last mobilisation, I think that the brigade was 3600 conscripts strong. I cannot say that for absolutely certain, but I think that the strength of the brigade was thereabouts after the last mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, upon your arrival at the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, did you actively join the work of the command as Chief of Staff, and did you carry out all of the functions normally attributed or assigned to the Chief of Staff, because up until that time you were out in the field.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived, there was a lot of work awaiting me there, since I was absent for quite a while from the brigade command. Thus I had to take care of some of the tasks which were not strictly necessary. I still had to do them and I had to check them to make sure that all of the documentation that is mandatory in wartime was properly kept and maintained. In addition to that, I had to familiarise myself with the most important activities in the preceding 50 months of the involvement of the brigade. Therefore, it was very demanding, the work that I had to do, and there was very little time for me to rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned some of the documents, the records that are kept in the brigade command. I suppose that among those documents is the war log, an operations log. Please tell me, who was in charge of that, and who monitored the entries made in these documents?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The documents at the brigade command, such as the operations log and war log book are maintained by an operations officer under the command of the Chief of Staff who just like -- who as chief of the operations organ with the -- within the command know about all the information that is entered into these very important wartime documents. For example, the war log book is permanently archived in the archives of the superior commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who made entries in the war log book of the 80th Motorised Brigade while you were in Vukovar in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was done by the officers from the operations organ, such as Captain Premovic, Teldasijevic [phoen], and other operations officers. There were four or five of them. I'm not quite sure right now, but four or five of them. And they were in charge of these two diaries. They made entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Premovic, can you tell us something about him, who was he what was had I his training and how was he trained?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Premovic is a reserve officer. I don't remember whether he was a Captain or Captain first class, but I think that he did this job conscientious. As far as I can remember he was an engineer and he used to work in a factory called Zastava, whether he works there to this day I don't know because I haven't had any contact with him for quite a long time. As for him, I can say that he was a very responsible, meticulous person. Now, whether he had the best possible training in terms of operations work, I don't know. But at any rate he did his best in order to carry out all of the assignments given to him in the most conscientious and responsible manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he complete the school for reserve officers and did he have to go frequently to additional training courses or manoeuvres in order to become Captain first class?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, he is a reserve officers. He graduated from the school for reserve officers. All of the officers of the command of the brigade normally go once or twice and some go even more often, once or twice a year, to attend what we called applied forms of training from various exercises to war simulation exercises, especially for staff tasks, which is the highest form of training for a senior officers and those belonging to commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether Major Jankovic also worked with the documents and tell me if you know this man.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Major Jankovic was the chief of operations organ and the only active officer within the operations organ. I can tell you that he was a good officer and that he did these tasks properly if I can say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we now -- could we now see another exhibit, please, which is the war log book of the 80th Brigade, 375. You have the hard copy before you. Could we have the English version on the screen, please. Could we see the entry for the 9th of November, at 2000 hours, which is page 0D 000571 in the English version. The entry here is 2100 hours, and LAD Artillery Battalion. Could we actually scroll down. We need the -- no, actually up. Could you scroll up. That's fine. That's fine. Where it says 2100 hours. It says as follows: "PVO LAD with two batteries, 20/3, is deployed in the Dubrava sector, and battery 30/2 in the Vucedol - Vukovar sector," correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What does this entry mean?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: It says here what the deployment of the LAD PVO was and this battery, 30/2 was deployed in the Vucedol sector so this was the deployment of the artillery battalion in terms of its batteries. At 2100 hours on the 9th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that it actually reflects the deployment of two PVO artillery battalions or rather their batteries. Which units did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: This was within the composition of the brigade. I don't see that they were resubordinated to anybody else, because that's what it says here in this war log book. Further down below, you see other units, HAD 105 and other units, staff units within the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like, now, to see the entry for the 10th of November at 1800 hours, which is page 74662. 1825. It says here: "LAD PVO is operating pursuant to the plan, and combat tasks of the OG South." And then next to it, it says: "Permanent tasks, or ongoing tasks." Can you tell us what kind of tasks these were? Permanent or ongoing combat tasks which were carried out in this particular case by LAD PVO, but this also pertained to other units within the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the brigade, the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade received an order in relation to the PVO as part of a additional, supplemental order within OG South where it is specified precisely which PVO formations are to participate in the anti-aircraft defence within the combat disposition of OG South, whose part the 80th Motorised Brigade was as well. Thus, this particular order pertains to the LAD PVO of the 80th Motorised Brigade in order to ensure unified engagement of all PVO units and the most efficient use of those units for anti-aircraft defence purposes. Ongoing or permanent tasks are defined in combat rules of the artillery battalion of the PVO as well as other combat rules on engagement of PVO resources. Ongoing tasks represent protection of facilities, weaponry, elements of combat disposition, those which are most vulnerable. The command of the brigade or the chief of the PVO within the 80th Motorised Brigade also had to write down, within the operations organ, an order for PVO and forward it to the commander of the LAD PVO of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that this order for PVO protection or PVO defence specified that the logistics support of the LAD Artillery Battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade on the 11th of November was to be conducted in OG South, and after that -- after the 18th of November it was to be carried out within the rear of the 80th Motorised Brigade, could you tell me what the reasons would be for such an order? Where was the rear of the 80th Motorised Brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 11th of November, 1991, the Logistics Battalion was on the move towards the sector of its deployment, that is to say from Smederevo to the village of Sotin, that is to say that the LAD PVO in relation to logistic support had to rely on the logistical structures of OG South. That was the only reason. I really don't see that there would be a different reason, nor do I know of a different reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this a good time for our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to four, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to move around the mics so that everybody can hear me better. And as for you, Mr. Danilovic, could you move away from the microphone a little bit, please, for the sake of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This courtroom is quite difficult. They have hard time hearing us. Thank you. I would like to continue with my examination. Mr. Danilovic, let us look at the entry in the operations diary, Exhibit 375. The date is 16th of November, time 1650. This is page 7 of the English text -- no, I apologise. No. This is Exhibit 371, page 7 of the English text. And as for you, you have the hard copy before you. Exhibit 371. Page 7 of the English translation. The entry made on the 16th of November, at 1650 hours. Mr. Danilovic, it says here: "From the 1st Motorised Battalion, Lieutenant Colonel Rade Danilovic returned and reported to the brigade commander on the situation in the 1st Motorised Battalion. The battalion is constantly in combat in the Luzac sector. They had fatalities and the wounded ..." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Just a second. Let me please find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is the operations log. Not the war log.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. I had the war log in front of me. Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, no, the operations log book. 16th of November at 1650 hours.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So did you come back at this time on this date as is entered here? And did you report to the commander on the situation in the first battalion?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. On that date, I returned from the 1st Motorised Battalion and I reported to the brigade commander on the situation in the battalion and on the losses. I can't remember, and I'm telling you this honestly, I can't remember the number of those who were killed and wounded. I know that there were both categories during combat when this battalion was engaged. In combat from the Djergaj forest towards the village of Luzac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could we turn to the next date, the 17th of November, once again, Exhibit 371, the entry made at 1800 hours. In English it is page 8. Thank you. In this entry, it says: "Commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade decided. Continue the operations of the third motorised battalion, reach the Vuka river and prevent the enemy from withdrawing from the northern part of Vukovar. Town of Vukovar. By means of engagement of the HAD and LAD PVO, support the breaking up of enemy forces in the northern part of Vukovar, establishing the most favourable conditions for the final liberation of Vukovar." Is that what it says in the operations log, and was this the order of the commander of the 80th Brigade issued to commanders of the 3rd Motorised Battalion HAD and LAD PVO of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's exactly how it was. This is how these three units were engaged in carrying out this portion of the combat order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, Mr. Danilovic, are you aware of the handover of the area of responsibility which took place between the 80th Partisan Brigade and the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, as Chief of Staff, and I was duty bound to know this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter'S correction. 20th Partisan Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, you as Chief of Staff, can you describe to us how a handover of the area of responsibility is carried out, so there are commands of two brigades which both find themselves within the area of responsibility of OG South?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The handover of the area of responsibility is carried out on the terrain, so that the outgoing unit leaves and the new unit arrives. The commanders at all levels have to be informed in detail about the disposition of the unit on the ground, so that those who are leaving, while leaving the area of combat disposition of the unit, have to be informed down to the last level, to the level of a squad, about the situation in that territory. The outgoing unit, its commander rather, has to inform the new commander in great detail as to where their support, equipment support weapons were deployed, and so on, as well as all details about the combat disposition of the unit, and what is most important, the information about the enemy and enemy units in that area. This means that the old commander is duty-bound to inform the new commander, in great detail, of all of these particulars and also issue an order on how the units are to be used in this area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see Exhibit 418. ERN 04672869. That's in B/C/S. And as for English, it should be 04672869 to 2871. Thank you. Can we see the bottom of the page, please. This is a daily combat report for the 19th of November, OG South, and in the last paragraph it says: Pursuant to your order, strictly confidential, number 1614/82-60, dated the 7th of November, 1991, commander of OG South, in his order, strictly confidential number 349-1, specifies the following local commands or town commands. Could we now see the next page on this document, please, which is page 04672870. Would you please look at item 3, village of Ovcara, Jakubovac, Grabovo, Lieutenant Colonel Misovic [phoen] Slobodan, and following his leading of the area of responsibility of OG South, Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Vojnovic is appointed. Do you remember this particular situation and when this took place?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact situation. I know that there was a handover of area of responsibility and that it was precisely along these lines, as stipulated in this order. But I can't remember all of the details, because it's been 15 years. I know that this order was implemented in its entirety, it was complied with in its entirety. And there was nothing contentious about it, but I can't remember the precise details of the handover of area of responsibility. All I know is that this order was complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at another entry regarding the 80th Brigade. I would like to see whether you remember this. In item 4, in the last paragraph on this page, on this page before us, it says: "In the course of the day tactical group of the 105th Motorised Brigade entered the composition of OG South with 450 men which was resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. Lieutenant Colonel Jovic was the commander of the 195th tactical group and he reported to Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, to receive assignment from him, and that's when we met. His operations officer copied the work map and the disposition of the units of the 80th Motorised Brigade so that this tactical group could be engaged in carrying out the tasks of the 80th Motorised Brigade. It was normal for the commander of this tactical group to know, in full, the combat disposition of the unit that he was joining.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Bearing in mind what we've been saying about local commands, or town commands, can you please look at a different document now, this is on the 65 ter list. It is ID 02 and the ERN is 0D 000466. The English is 0467. That's the first document in the set of documents that was distributed at the start of day. This is an order that Commander Vojnovic signed. What exactly does it say, if you could please comment for our benefit, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order by the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade regulating the respective authorities in terms of local commands or villages or settlements. In this case, it's the commander of the logistics battalion, but rather he hereby appointed him commander of Sotin village, Captain First Class Nemanja Jankovic, his own deputy, and Sergeant Dragan Todorovic as a member of the command, thereby setting up a local command for Sotin village where the logistics battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade was stationed. Item 2 regulates their respective responsibilities. Do you want me to comment on that too in terms of the local command?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us what exactly the local commands are supposed to do based on this order?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Local commanders or the commanders of these villages were ordered to organise proper authorities in keeping with the rules of the armed forces, and provisions governing the service in barracks and garrisons. They were also ordered to take all measures to prevent any incursions by sabotage or terrorist groups or any terrorist action. If you look at item 2 it says: Draw up appropriate instructions for work and ensure normal conditions for the life and work of the local population. It is of paramount importance to foil any mistreatment against the local population, or any unauthorized entry and search of flats and houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, can you just tell me one thing. This portion that is in reference to the rules of service in barracks and garrisons, you say that is part of this order. What I want to know is, based on these rules of service, who is it that defines the rules of detention at a local command? Who defines the necessary security measures?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: That is down to the local commander, the commander of a town or village, whoever is tasked with carrying out these assignments. They must set a place of detention and sort everything else out in keeping with that. It is certainly the local commander who is responsible to regulate everything in keeping with the rules governing the work of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 767, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we now, please, have Exhibit 375, this is the war log, specifically the entry in relation to the 11th of November, 1,200 hours. In the English this is page 10. This is the war log. Indeed, I think the witness has the B/C/S in front of him, so maybe we could bring the English up in our monitors. That would be better for the benefit of the Chamber. I'm talking about page 10. The witness has both in hard copy and should be able to find his way around. The page number is 10 in the English. The entry is in relation to the 11th [as interpreted] of November, 1800 hours. There's an error in the transcript. It says the 11th, and it should be the 18th. The 18th of November. Page 30, line 15. The English pages stand. Page 10. Excellent. Thank you. Do you see this entry right there, sir? It says: "Vukovar has been liberated. JNA operations ceased at eleven o'clock and the elements of our brigade on the right bank of the Vuka river as well as those from the Milovo Brdo sector. Hostilities were suspended. A surrender of the Ustasha forces in the Mitnica sector and Vukovar Hospital has been announced. 1,200 hours Captain first class Premovic. Isn't that what it says in the operations log, rather the war log? Do you remember an assignment like this being issued?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I most certainly do. There was a lot of shooting, soldiers and some of the officers welcomed the end of these hostilities with great joy. And everything else from this point on would have been much easier to sort out. I remember the time when Vukovar eventually fell and when all units and operations carried out by these units involved in liberating Vukovar ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you look at the first portion of this entry, it's in relation to the armed operations ceasing as well as those that applied to members of your brigade, right? If you look at the continuation of that entry, you see that a surrender of the Ustasha forces is expected. Did your brigade have any sort of involvement at all in what is addressed in the last portion of this entry?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the brigade commander drew our attention to the fact that we had to be prepared to take over the captured forces of the National Guards Corps and the MUP and to make sure they were safe until they were evacuated and sent on to collection centres for further processing and investigations. Likewise our attention was drawn to the fact that there would be individual evacuations carried out for groups that had not surrendered to OG South or any of its units. He said there was a danger that the brigade might suffer losses by these Ustasha forces that are left behind. Losses might be suffered as they were pulling out of the city of Vukovar, he said. Furthermore, units of OG South wanted to be rid of this in the manner of speaking, because when prisoners were being taken it was the remaining elements of OG South that bore the brunt of the operation, so to speak. The brigade had a lot less to do as far as this was concerned. But it had to secure the prisoners until they were evacuated, had to make sure they were safe and out of the theatre of war as well as to prepare them for further processing or vetting the normal procedure that is applied to POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you received this assignment, at headquarters, did you draw up a plan about warning your units, in terms of their obligation to implement international rules of war?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: It has been a long time, and as far as I remember several orders were written, detailed ones, to the effect that the Geneva Conventions were to be complied with, and this especially concerned the treatment of POWs. At the brigade command, we had a special rule enshrining all these provisions. I think all of the JNA units involved in combat operations were aware of this rule, and aware of their obligation to apply it. However, in addition to just simply having this rule, separate orders were written, specific ones, and that is obvious if you look at orders issued by unit commands during the attack on Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just interrupt for one moment? I don't criticize my learned friend in any way at all but phrases like the brigade commanders or the brigade commander is used. I wonder if it's possible for my learned friend to use the name of the individual to whom that refers, so that it assists all parties when they look at the, at the transcript either now or later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my learned friend. I said the brigade command. I didn't say the brigade commanders. I said the brigade command, as a collective body with all sorts of different assignments. Nevertheless I will be asking the witness a more detailed question about this and a more straightforward one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As far as this issue was concerned, which steps did the OG South command take and which steps did the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade take? And do you know what steps were taken by the command of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: What I can say is that the command of the 1st Military District as far as the POWs were concerned, issued an order which was received by OG South. An order was then written and sent to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, according to which the 80th Motorised Brigade was required to have all the items contained and the order implemented as far as treatment of POWs was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me just clarify what you shared with us a while ago in your previous answer. Not this one. This was done at the brigade command level. Which brigade, did you have in mind? Just to make it perfectly clear here.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade, that's the one I had in mind, as well as all other brigade units, lower level units such as assault detachments, and all other units that were involved in the implementation of this attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In terms of the application of international humanitarian law, was this ever brought up at any of the daily briefings at the headquarters of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade commanders, whenever battalion and division commanders came to a briefing, on several occasions focused on this issue pointing out its importance, with the objective of preventing any violations of the Geneva Conventions or the international lore [as interpreted] of war from occurring. I can't say how many times he drew the officer's attention to this, but one thing that I'm certain about is it happened on a number of different occasions, and not just once.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A while ago we were talking about one of the entries in the war log, the 80th Brigade was assigned the task of making sure that the prisoners were received and safe on the 18th of November, 1991. Can we now look at the same war log, the same page, the entry in relation to the 19th of November, at 1800 hours. In the English it is the same page. Page 10. Down towards the bottom of the page. Thank you. It reads: During the morning hours the Ustasha were taken to the Sremska prison. The fighting continues in the hospital sector only where the remains of the ZNG and MUP are expected to surrender. (About 200) an order was issued to be prepared to organise the guarding of prisoners. End of quote. Do you remember an order like this coming in relation to the 19th November. It arrived on the 19th of November at 1800 hours. Do you remember an announcement like this?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember an order saying that preparations were to be carried out in order to receive this new group of captured members of the Z N G and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you involved when this first group that was announced on the 18th of November at 1,200 hours was received, and did you secure that group? Were you required to do anything about that first group?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed by the brigade commander to be the POW camp commander at the village of Ovcara. The first group, the group that was the first to arrive, comprised about 70 members of the ZNG and the MUP. Later on, I think another 100 or 110 prisoners were brought to the hanger at this farm, at the Ovcara farm. In addition to myself, the camp commander, nearly all the other staff officers were involved. I mean the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade as well as elements of the military police company and a reconnaissance company. I remember it was night time and the night-time was an exceptionally cold one. We set up a length of rope in that hangar, beyond which the prisoners were not allowed to move. On the other side of this length of rope there were officers or guards, two soldiers, one officer, two soldiers one officer with their weapons at the ready, at the far end, were stacks of hay, there was one person in particular and the prisoners seemed to have him as the person in charge and he asked for the stacks of Hay to be given them to keep them war which I allowed at the time. Later on I became slightly concerned even thinking what might happen if any of them had a lighter on or a box of matches and decided to set fire to those stacks of hay, in order to stage an escape or something like that. Given the cold weather, however, you had to be a proper human being and do something for those people, regardless of the fact there may be criminals among them. Likewise, we made sure that they had cans or vessels for passing water that night it was minus three, minus for our perhaps even minus five. It was a very cold night and that's the reason I remember all of these specifics as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me just clarify about this group of prisoners that we're talking about now. Where did they come from? Where were they brought from? Which part of Vukovar? Be?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I it was it was our security people who had brought them over from Mitnica, if I remember correctly. I had I they were from the Mitnica sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just another question about this. You talked about the involvement of the brigade command officers, in addition to the military police company and the reconnaissance company. Roughly speaking how many brigade command officers were involved in this assignment and I know you can't remember everything specifically but which posts or positions did they hold in the command at the time, these people who were involved?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: There were between 10 and 12 of them involved but I'm afraid I can't be more specific than that. It has been a very long time. For the most part those were officers from the Staff, operative officers, chiefs of branches, and services. Together with me these people were required to make sure the prisoners were safe until an officer came along to take them away and take them to Sremska Mitrovica with all new security measures being applied. If I remember correctly Sremska Mitrovic was one of the POW collection centres at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have a deputy, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It's just that the name escapes me, I can't remember who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What if I tell you it was Stanimir Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: That's it, that's right. The name just slipped my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How many shifts were envisaged, shifts of soldiers and officers to secure the being hangar with the POWs?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I think there were two shifts rotating. I was required to be there throughout and I was until this whole tribulation was over, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did you say two shifts? Two shifts rotating? Did I get that right?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were two shifts rotating all the time. Perhaps there were two hour shifts, perhaps less, perhaps more. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell us if you spent the entire night with these POWs, annexed to them? Or were you also on rotation, as it were? You would be on shift for a while, then you would rest.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I was there throughout in that building. I simply had to be there with both shifts. This responsibility rested squarely on my shoulders and I felt its burden. I made to make sure those people were safe, and dually taken to the Sremska Mitrovica POW centre, to the best of my recollection I was there throughout, but it's very difficult to be dead on simply because it has been such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you secure a spot where those members of your units, who were not on a shift at the time, could keep warm, those who were trying to enter the rotation system?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I really can't say anything about that. I can't remember if they had a place to keep warm, or not. I assume they would have been able to light a fire and warm up a little. Those who were resting. Those who were guarding the prisoners were certainly not able to take advantage of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Throughout your time there were there any problems regarding the prisoners, or was everything calm throughout?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember this man in charge -- and I can't remember his name -- I told him to come over and I said to him, "Please don't try anything stupid. You or any of your men. Don't try to escape or anything like that because you'll be fired at." As far as that was concerned, there were no problems whatsoever. There should be witnesses to confirm that, witnesses from that group. The group that was put up at the Ovcara farm. Well, as long as they're honest about it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that there were no problems with them. Did the security have problems with anyone from the outside trying to enter the hangar?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I think there were no such problems, either. As far as I remember. I think that a group of police officers from OG South at a certain time arrived to check whether everything was all right, but they stayed very briefly at that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you present when they arrived? Or did you just hear, hear of it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did they say why they had arrived? And did they -- did they speak to you at all?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that they only asked whether there had been any problems and that was it. They left. They had only asked whether there had been any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to have another look at the operation log, Exhibit 371, the entry dated 18th of November, 14 hours 10 minutes on page 8, the English version. And you, sir, you have the B/C/S version in front of you. Let's just wait for it to appear on our screens. I repeat, Exhibit 371, on page 8 in the English translation. The date is November 18th and the time 14 hours 10 minutes. Scroll down a little, please. Thank you. At 14 hours ten minutes on November 18th, order was -- an order was passed for all officers and some soldiers of the reconnaissance unit, the communications company and another unit to line up. They had all -- they all went to the Ovcara farm in Vukovar and their task was to organise a camp for putting up the captured members of the MUP and ZNG from Croatian at the Mitnica sector. Mitnica area. Is this what the operation log says?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. That's exactly what it says, and that's what it was like, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to continue with the entry at 1600 hours on the same day. The first group was taken by trucks around 7 see persons, 70, 70 Ustasha were put into detention. During the night, another 100 or so were brought. Lieutenant Colonel Rade Danilovic was appointed commander of the camp, and almost all officers of the brigade command were involved in the security. Mr. Danilovic, is this what the operations log says and does this correspond to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That's what happened. I think that's -- I said so a minute ago. I don't think it's necessary for me to repeat, but this is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now continue with the entry at 1800 hours on the same day, this is on the following page, 9 for the English version. The B/C/S version is on the same page. So this is November 18th, 1991 at 1800 hours. It says: A report was sent to the Corps Command with the explanation of the fall of Vukovar and the details of the surrender of the Ustasha. Day and night duty was ordered at the Ovcara farm. Is this what it says and is this what you remember? And tell us to which Corps this report was sent.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what it says. As far as I remember, this was sent to the command of the 24th Corps, to which the 80th Motorised Brigade belongs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, before we continue, what the following date -- about the reports, the security reports and reports of the completion of tasks, to who did you report about all of that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I only reported to Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, the brigade commander, who had given me my assignment, I think that is logical. And in accordance with the line of command, he reported to superior commands about the completion of these assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the same Exhibit, 375, I would like to take a look at the next entry --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the date, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- at 800 hours. "Duty still uninterrupted at the camp in Ovcara prison." Is this what it says, Mr. Danilovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, that's what the log reads. So the date is the 19th of November at 800 hours, 19th of November, 800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And now let's please look at the entry at 1,200 hours on the -- on the 19th November, which says: We were informed that a decision was taken that the captured members of the ZNG be transferred to Sremska Mitrovica. Lieutenant Colonel Danilovic was relieved from the responsibility concerning the guarding of the captured MUP and ZNG members in the Ovcara sector. Mr. Danilovic, can you explain, based on what you remember, can you explain this entry?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: According to my recollection, the commander relieved me from this duty to send me to the 2nd Motorised Battalion with some other officers from the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade to accomplish the next mission, because there were great problems in that area. There was one dead or two, and six or seven wounded soldiers. I think that parts of the 1st and 2nd Company had deserted their positions without an order, and gone to Nemci, because that battalion, as far as I remember, had joined the 3rd Mechanised Guard Brigade there, if I remember well. And there were big problems there, and that's why, as far as I remember, the commander had sent me to accomplish a mission there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just tell me where you were supposed to go, and on which day, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to go with a group of officers, which, apart from me, included the commander of the Pioneers, then there were two Captains from the morale organ. I think the name of one of them was Radosadovic [phoen]. I don't remember the names now, and I think I was supposed to, to report about the situation in the battalion, and warn them that they should accomplish their assignments in the coming period, and that a special focus was to be put on that, because on the 15th and 16th through the 18th of November, a unit was massacred by the members of the ZNG and MUP from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Danilovic. Let's come back to this assignment of yours when you reach it in the operations log. Before you left to accomplish your mission, the operations log on the 19th of November, at 2300 hours, the English version is on page 10, reads that the commander of the 80th Brigade had issued orders regarding the commander of the site. Do you remember who he appointed?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: According to this document, it says exactly that the commander of the village of Ovcara was Captain First Class Jan Marcek and as commander of LAD PVO his deputy was Captain First Class Milisav Drazic. This is a xerox copy, which is not so easily legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the brigade commander at the same time appoint commanders of the villages of Grabovo and Jakubovac?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the relief of the partisan unit, the Captain Misevic, or whatever his name, was substituted by Lieutenant Colonel Jovic of the 25th tactical group, and he was to appoint the persons responsible to him for the villages of Jakubovac and Grabovo as far as the organisation of the duties that must be in place at inhabited settlements are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph of this entry reads that the: Order had been typed and signed by 2330 minutes and "will be delivered early tomorrow morning". Is this what it says?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would now like to take a look at Exhibit 369. Exhibit 369 it's an order of the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade. It reads: "Strogo pova," dated November 20th, 1991. So you can see the English version on the screen, and we also need the B/C/S version. So this is marked D 000537. Let us zoom in on that. Mr. Danilovic, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is this the order of the commander of the 80th Brigade by which he appoints Jan Marcek commander of Ovcara village?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It reads: I appoint Jan Marcek commander of the village of Ovcara, and I appoint as a substitute Captain First Class Drazic Milisav. The other members of the command will be appointed by the village commander. This is item 1 -- oh, yes, now I can see it better. In the village mentioned, law and order have to be organised in accordance with rules of service in the armed forces and the relevant provisions that pertain to garrison and barracks service, as well as take on measures directed at the prevention of incursions of terrorists, terrorist groups and sabotage groups and prevent them from conducting terrorist actions. Draw up instructions for work and ensure normal life conditions for the, for the inhabitants. It also says, prevent all occasion -- all occurrences of the mistreatment of the local population. Is this, content-wise, equal to the orders that we have seen in Exhibit 767 that refers to the village of Sotin?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Content wise, it is the same. Only this is directed to Captain first class Jan Marcek, from LAD PVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would now like to take a look at Exhibit 373. The date is marked OD 000533. So 533. Mr. Danilovic, we needn't read this out again. Just have a look at this order, if you please, and tell us whether this order -- well, this is the order by which Lieutenant Colonel Milan Jovic is appointed, the commander of Grabovo and Jakubovac?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same order. Only it applies to these two villages and it mentions Lieutenant Colonel Jovic and the commander of the 195th tactical group, but the content is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The number of this order is 32- 2. Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of 20th November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please do not talk at the same time. We cannot interpret both.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please, I would now like to have on the screen a document from the 65 ter list marked ID 03. This is the second in the set of handouts that I distributed to everybody. The ERN number is 0D 000537. For you, sir, the information is that the, that this is the second document in the sequence; 1D 03. Number 3. This is the strictly classified order 34-2. Would you kindly take a look at this order, Mr. Danilovic and tell us what Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Vojnovic ordered here and when.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: This strictly confidential order, 34- 2, dated 27th -- the 22nd of November, says that the command should be organised in the villages of Grabovo, Jakubovac and Ovcara and that the commander of the 195th tactical group would appoint the commanders, namely one said command for Jakubovac and Ovcara and another site command for the village of Grabovo. This is what item 1 of that order says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We have to repeat the date, so this is page 46, line 3. The date is November 22nd, rather than "27th".

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The 22nd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Take a look at item 2, please, sir, don't read it out. Tell me whether it -- it has the same content as the other items and the all previous orders appointing the site commanders?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's identical to all previous orders. Only this has another added item, item 3, which says that this order overrules the order dated November 20th, 1991, number 32-2, and 32-3. Strictly confidential. This is added as item 3 in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please explain to us why the commander of the 80th Brigade, by this order, overruled the previous order. Is this normal procedure when issuing orders, or not.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the commander had his reasons for changing this order. I really cannot remember for sure what his basic motive was. At any rate, if an order is changed, it must be replaced by a new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you say that this is standard procedure when replacing one order by another?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: It happens that under some circumstances new orders must be passed. I can give examples that have nothing to do with this concrete case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We're only interested in the procedure. If the commander replaces one order by another, does he overrule the previous one?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. You cannot have two orders on the same thing at the same time, because that would -- that would mean great problems for units in the performance of their combat tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to tender this into evidence, this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 777, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].
